articoli.titolo: From 8,000 Spots to a World of Folks
articoli.estratto: The story behind SpotFolk: how a personal collection of places became an idea for a different kind of community.
articoli.testo:
It started with a map.

Over the years, I had collected more than 8,000 locations around the world. Places I had discovered through remote scouting, hours spent exploring satellite images, maps, travel blogs and geographical details, but also through personal experiences, road trips and time spent out in the field.

Some were hidden viewpoints, others forgotten villages, quiet roads, mountain trails, unusual architectural details or simply places that made me stop and look twice.

Each location had something that caught my attention. And gradually, the collection became something much bigger than a personal archive.

I called them *Spots*.

## An obsession with finding places

Finding interesting locations has always been part of the way I approach photography and travelling.

Sometimes, discovering a place starts long before actually getting there. I can spend hours exploring a remote area on a map, following a road that seems to lead nowhere, looking for an unusual coastline or trying to understand how the light might interact with a particular landscape.

Other times, a Spot comes from a completely different experience: a place I stumble upon while travelling, a recommendation from someone, or a location that surprises me when I least expect it.

Remote scouting and real-world exploration eventually became two sides of the same process.

The result was a growing collection of thousands of places, each with its own potential story.

At some point, I started thinking: why should all these discoveries remain mine?

## From my map to everyone's map

My first idea was quite simple: make the map public and allow other people to explore my collection.

I wanted to share those 8,000 Spots with photographers, travellers and curious people looking for somewhere different to go.

But the more I thought about it, the more I realised that simply opening my map wasn't enough.

There are millions of interesting places in the world, and no single person could ever discover them all.

What if other people could contribute their own discoveries?

What if a photographer could share a viewpoint, a hiker could add a trail, a traveller could recommend a little village, and someone passionate about food could introduce a place worth travelling for?

The map could become something that grows with its community.

Not just a collection of places, but a shared collection of discoveries.

And that changed everything.

## Then came the Folks

The next question was: who are the people behind these places?

Most platforms organise places around ratings, reviews and stars. You visit somewhere, leave a score, write a few lines and move on.

But I always felt something was missing.

A five-star rating doesn't tell me much about the person who gave it. It doesn't tell me what they were looking for, what caught their attention or why they decided that a particular place was worth sharing.

I wanted something more personal.

That's where the idea of the *Folk* came from.

Every user becomes a Folk. Every Spot can carry the signature of the person who discovered it or chose to share it.

A photographer, a hiker, a foodie, a traveller, a digital nomad: different people, different interests, different ways of looking at the world.

And each of them brings something unique to the map.

The interesting part is no longer just the place itself. It's the person behind the discovery.

## Less about stars. More about signatures.

I don't think places need another endless competition of ratings and reviews.

What makes a location interesting is often much more subjective than a number.

A hidden viewpoint might be extraordinary to a landscape photographer. A quiet mountain refuge might mean everything to a hiker. A tiny restaurant might become someone's favourite discovery of an entire journey.

None of these experiences needs to be validated by a five-star rating.

Sometimes, knowing who recommends a place is far more valuable than knowing how many stars it has.

That's the idea behind SpotFolk: **your signature makes the Spot worth discovering.**

Not because every recommendation has to be perfect, but because every discovery comes from a real person with their own perspective.

## A map that belongs to everyone

SpotFolk is still built around the original idea: discovering interesting places and making them easier to find.

But it has evolved into something more ambitious.

I started with more than 8,000 Spots collected over years of scouting and exploration. Today, I want to see that map grow through the eyes of thousands of different people.

I don't want it to be just my map anymore.

I want it to become a place where photographers, travellers, hikers, food lovers and curious minds can leave their mark, share what they find and discover the world through someone else's eyes.

Because the world doesn't need another list of the best places.

It needs more people willing to share the places they love.

And every Spot deserves a Folk behind it.

## Around the fire, there's room for you.

Every great journey is better when shared.

And every good story deserves an audience.

I imagine SpotFolk as a campfire somewhere in the world. A place where people with different backgrounds, passions and experiences gather to share the places they've discovered, the paths they've taken and the stories they've collected along the way.

Some come with photographs. Others with hiking trails, favourite food spots, hidden villages or simply a curiosity to explore.

It doesn't matter what kind of Folk you are. What matters is what you bring to the circle.

So, pull up a seat. There's room around the fire.

**Come join the Folks. Discover new places, share your own Spots and leave your signature on the map.**

The fire is already burning. We're just waiting for you.

**[Join SpotFolk → spotfolk.eu](https://spotfolk.eu)**

articoli.slug: A practical field guide to camera settings, exposure bracketing and capturing the full dynamic range of a night scene.
articoli.estratto: A practical field guide to camera settings, exposure bracketing and capturing the full dynamic range of a night scene.
articoli.testo:
## 1. Understand the three exposure parameters

Before shooting at night, you need to understand what each parameter does. The goal is not simply to get more light, but to control how that light is recorded.


| Parameter | What it controls | What happens when you increase it |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| **Aperture (f/)** | Amount of light and depth of field | More light, less depth of field |
| **Shutter speed** | How long the sensor receives light | More light, but more motion blur |
| **ISO** | Sensor sensitivity to the signal | Brighter image, but potentially more noise |


A wide aperture (e.g. f/2.8) lets in more light but reduces depth of field. A smaller aperture (e.g. f/8) gives you greater depth of field and helps keep the scene sharp from foreground to background, but requires longer exposure times.

A slower shutter captures more light, but moving subjects may become blurred.

ISO is useful when you need to increase brightness without extending exposure time. However, higher ISO generally means more noise, particularly in the shadows.

**The key is to balance all three according to the scene you're photographing.**

## 2. Recover the full dynamic range

Night photography often presents a difficult challenge: very bright artificial lights alongside extremely dark areas.

A single exposure rarely captures all the information we need. Streetlights, illuminated buildings and shop windows can easily become overexposed, while shadows lose detail.

My solution is to capture a sequence of exposures, gradually covering the entire dynamic range of the scene.

This gives us different frames to work with later: some preserve the highlights, others reveal the shadows.

There are two ways to do this.

### Method A – Exposure Bracketing (AEB)

For most urban scenes, this is my preferred method.

I usually work in **Aperture Priority mode (A)**, so I can keep the aperture fixed and let the camera adjust shutter speed between exposures.

My typical starting setup in the city is:

- 5 bracketed exposures.
- A range starting at -3 EV.
- The aperture remains fixed throughout the sequence.

The exact exposure spacing can be adjusted according to the scene's dynamic range.

This approach is quick, reliable and usually provides enough information to recover both highlights and shadows.

If the scene is particularly contrasty, simply extend the sequence with additional exposures.

### Method B – Manual exposure

For distant villages and complex landscapes, I prefer working in Manual mode.

Think of places such as Manarola, photographed from a distant viewpoint. Here, I want greater control over every exposure, especially when the scene contains many different light sources and large areas of darkness.

My usual sequence follows this order:

**1. Start with the shadows.**

I begin by exposing the darkest areas, making sure I capture all the details I might need.

I prefer keeping ISO at its native value whenever possible and using longer exposures, even Bulb mode if necessary. If the exposure time becomes impractical, I may increase ISO.

Sometimes, more than one exposure is needed to capture the darkest areas properly.

**2. Gradually move towards the midtones.**

Once I have the shadow information, I start building the rest of the sequence.

I progressively close the aperture, usually reaching f/7 or f/8, to obtain sufficient depth of field and good overall sharpness.

**3. Recover the highlights.**

I then progressively shorten the shutter speed, capturing additional exposures until the brightest lights are properly preserved.

This gives me a gradual sequence of exposures, from the darkest areas to the brightest highlights.

**4. Photograph the sky separately.**

If the sky is visible and contains stars, I take a dedicated exposure for it.

For sharp stars, I use the 500 rule as a quick starting point:

**Maximum shutter speed ≈ 500 ÷ focal length (full-frame equivalent).**

For more accurate results, particularly with high-resolution cameras, the NPF rule is preferable.

## 3. Don't forget moving subjects

There is one more shot I almost always recommend adding to your sequence.

A dedicated exposure for anything that moves.

Think about leaves moving in the wind, people walking through the scene, flowing water or branches moving during a long exposure.

These elements can create inconsistencies when combining different exposures.

Take an additional frame with the shutter speed appropriate for freezing the movement. You can then use it as a reference or source when blending the final image.

## 4. A small detail that makes a big difference: remote shooting

Whenever possible, I recommend controlling your camera remotely.

I use **Shutter on my iPhone** to trigger exposures without touching the camera.

Why does it matter?

When shooting long exposure sequences or exposure brackets, even a small movement can cause misalignment between frames.

A remote trigger helps keep the camera perfectly still and makes the entire process more reliable.

It's a small habit that can save you a lot of work later.

## 5. Which method should you use?

Here's my general rule:


| Situation | My recommendation |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Urban night photography | 5-shot exposure bracketing |
| Very high contrast city scenes | Bracketing with additional exposures |
| Distant villages and landscapes | Manual exposure sequence |
| Complex scenes with bright lights and deep shadows | Manual exposure sequence |
| Night sky with stars | Dedicated sky exposure |


You don't always need a complicated sequence. In most urban situations, a simple exposure bracket will give you everything you need.

For distant villages, however, I prefer Manual mode because it gives me much greater control over the entire process.

---

**Remember:** The goal isn't to get the perfect photograph in a single exposure. It's to capture all the information you need to create the perfect photograph later.

articoli.titolo: Do you know where and how to find Foliage?
articoli.estratto: Every autumn guide gives you a week. The colour does not work that way: it is a band of altitude that walks downhill, about 200 metres a week. Here is how to find the band before you drive.
articoli.testo:
## 1. The calendar is the wrong tool

Every autumn guide gives you a week. Mid-October for the Dolomites, early November for the Apennines. Then you drive four hours and find bare branches, or a wall of green.

The week is not wrong. It is answering a different question.

Autumn colour is not something that happens to a region on a date. It is a **band of altitude that walks downhill**, from the treeline to the valley floor, over roughly six weeks. On the same morning, in the same valley, you can have bare larch at 1,700 m, copper beech at 1,200 m and full green at 600 m.

So the question worth asking is not *when does this valley turn*. It is: **what height is the colour at today, and where can I stand inside that band?**

That question has an answer you can work out the night before, with free data and about ten minutes.


## 2. What sets the clock, and what only nudges it

Two forces, and it matters a great deal which is which.

**Day length sets the schedule.** As the days shorten, trees stop making chlorophyll and begin pulling back what they can from the leaf before letting it go. The yellows were always in there, masked by the green. This part is astronomy, not weather: it repeats every year within a few days, and you can count on it.

**Temperature turns the dial.** Sunny days keep sugar production going in the leaf; cool nights slow the movement of that sugar back out of it. The surplus is what becomes the red and purple pigments. The best displays come from bright days and cold but **frost-free** nights. A warm, wet autumn gives you muted yellows instead of reds. A hard frost, a gale, or two days of heavy rain do not improve anything — they end it.

For planning, that splits neatly in two:

- the **schedule** is roughly fixed, so altitude and the date tell you where the band should be;
- the **weather of the last two weeks** tells you whether you are early, late, or already too late.


## 3. The rule you can do in your head

In 1918 the American entomologist Andrew D. Hopkins published what became known as the bioclimatic law. He had been studying when things happen in nature across a continent, and he put it at four days for each degree of latitude, five degrees of longitude, and 400 feet — about 120 metres — of altitude. Later going north and going up in spring; and, crucially for us, **the same intervals earlier in autumn**.

It is a rough law, built on mass observation, and it has been argued over for a century. But as a field rule for foliage it is remarkably serviceable:

| Difference in height | Shift in the colour |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| **120 m higher** | about 4 days earlier |
| **250 m higher** | about a week earlier |
| **500 m higher** | about two weeks earlier |
| **1,000 m higher** | about a month earlier |

Turn it around and you get the number that actually plans your autumn:

> **The colour descends about 200 metres a week.**

Which means one observation gives you the whole season. If you saw peak colour at 1,500 m on 20 October, then around 10 November the band is near 900 m, and by the end of the month it is in the valley floors and the towns. One drive, noted down, and you can plan the next six weekends.


## 4. What overrides the rule

Three things, and all three are worth more than the arithmetic.

**Species.** Altitude tells you where the band is; the trees tell you how long it stays.

| Tree | Usual band | How it behaves |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Larch** | 1,400–2,200 m | Turns gold, then drops within days of the first hard frost. The shortest window and the biggest reward. |
| **Beech** | 900–1,500 m | Copper and orange, and it holds dead leaves for weeks. The forgiving one — and the one most likely to sit outside its band, as section 6 shows. |
| **Chestnut** | 500–900 m | Deep gold, late, and the forest floor matters as much as the canopy. |
| **Oak** | below 800 m | Brown, very late, often the last thing still holding. |
| **Poplar and willow** | valley floors | Yellow, late, and the first to be stripped by wind. |
| **Vineyards** | 200–600 m | Their own clock, by variety. Usually early to mid November. |

If you have one free weekend and the forecast is uncertain, go to beech. Larch punishes a week's delay; beech forgives it.

**Cold air sinks.** On clear, still nights cold air pools in the valley bottom, which can be several degrees colder than the slope 300 m above it. That is why you sometimes find a valley floor already turned while the hillside above is still green — the opposite of what the altitude rule predicts. Any enclosed basin or flat valley head is a candidate.

**Wind and rain end it early.** The rule tells you when the leaves colour. It says nothing about whether they are still attached. A single day of strong wind after a peak can empty a wood.


## 5. The three checks before you drive

All three are free, and together they take ten minutes.

**1. Find the first frost.** This is the single most useful number. Pull the daily minimum temperatures for the area over the last six weeks from any open weather archive and find the first night at or below zero, then the first at or below about −3 °C. Larch above that point is on a countdown of days. Below it, nothing has been forced yet.

**2. Find the snow line.** Regional bulletins give the height of recent snowfalls. Snow that fell above your band is scenery; snow that fell *on* it has closed it. The freezing level for the coming days tells you whether that is about to change.

**3. Count the wind and the rain.** Look at the last ten days. A mild, still fortnight preserves a peak well past the date you would predict. Two windy days remove it.

Then add the obvious one: a webcam. A single current frame from anywhere near your altitude beats any model — including this one. Read the webcam with your own eyes rather than trusting an automatic estimate: fog, backlight, and a dusting of snow on the lens fool software, not people.


## 6. A worked example: one mountain, three bands

Monte Cimino, in the Tuscia, a couple of hours north of Rome. A good example for two reasons: everything is within twenty minutes of driving, and the mountain breaks the rule in a way that teaches you how to use it.

The summit reaches 1,053 m, the highest point of the Cimini range and of the whole province of Viterbo. The old beech wood on top runs for about 58 hectares between 925 m and the summit, and since 2017 it has been part of the UNESCO site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. Some of the trees are over two centuries old and among the tallest beeches in Europe.

Now the interesting part. In central Italy, beech normally starts higher than this — you expect it above 1,200 m. Here it grows two or three hundred metres lower than it should, which is why it is called a *faggeta depressa*, a lowered beech wood. The reason is entirely local: volcanic soil among the most fertile in central Italy, high rainfall, and humid air arriving from the lake country below. Cool and wet, at a height where it has no business being either.

Read that as a planning fact rather than trivia:

> **Where a species sits below its usual band, the local climate has already moved the clock. Apply the rule to what actually grows there, not to the number on the map.**

The Cimino beech behaves roughly like beech three hundred metres higher in the Apennines — which puts its best week in the first half of November rather than late October.

Three bands, then, on the single road climbing from Soriano nel Cimino at 509 m:

| Band | Height | What grows there | Roughly when it turns |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Summit beech wood** | 925–1,053 m | Old *Fagus sylvatica*, 30 to 50 m tall | First half of November: yellow, copper, red-brown |
| **Chestnut slopes** | 500–900 m | Chestnut and hazel groves | Mid to late November — the chestnut festival in Soriano is in October, the colour comes after it |
| **Tuscia plain** | 300–500 m | Oak, vineyard, olive | Late November into December |

Seven hundred metres of altitude. By the rule in section 3 that is around three and a half weeks of difference, so one road gives you most of a month of autumn. Which is the real payoff of thinking in bands rather than dates: if the faggeta is past its best when you arrive, you do not drive home. You drive **down** three hundred metres and photograph something that is peaking that same morning.

Practical notes, if you go: the walkers' car park sits at about 970 m, and from there an easy loop of roughly two kilometres and a hundred metres of ascent — an hour, no difficulty — takes you through the big beeches and past the Sasso Menicante, the volcanic boulder that rocks when you push it.

One caution about the table. Those are the normal windows, not a forecast for this year: a hard frost in the last week of October, or two days of strong wind, moves everything. The windows tell you where to point; the three checks in section 5 tell you whether this particular autumn is running early or late.


## 7. The routine, in five lines

1. Decide the **band**: last known peak, minus 200 m for every week since.
2. Pick **species** inside that band — beech if your date is uncertain, larch only if it is not.
3. Check the **first frost** date for that height.
4. Check the **snow line** and the **wind** of the last ten days.
5. Look at a **webcam** the evening before, and keep the alternative 300 m lower in your pocket.


## 8. And once you are there

Do not wish for blue sky. An overcast day is the best light that exists for colour inside a wood: no hotspots, no black shadows, and the yellows hold their saturation. Save the clear mornings for backlight, which is the one thing that makes a larch or a beech genuinely glow — shoot into the sun, low, with the leaves between you and it.

For the rest, sunrise and sunset times for the day you are going, and what the light is doing right now, are in the planner on this site.

And when you get home, write down one line: the date, the height, and what you found. Do that for three autumns and you will stop needing the rule at all.

articoli.titolo: How to Photograph a City with a Fixed 50mm
articoli.estratto: A fifty does nothing for you: it cannot reach, and it cannot forgive where you stood. Four walks in Rome, and the four things it makes you do instead.
articoli.testo:
*The lens in this piece, a 7Artisans AF 50mm f/1.8, was provided as part of a collaboration in October 2026. The photographs and the judgements are mine.*

## 1. The focal length that refuses to help you

A fifty is the hardest prime to use well, and the reason is simple: it does almost nothing for you.

A wide angle forgives a badly chosen position, because it takes in everything and lets you sort it out later. A telephoto picks the subject out of the mess and hands it to you. Fifty millimetres does neither. It sees roughly what your eye sees, at roughly the scale your eye sees it, so the frame contains exactly what you were standing in front of — no more, no less.

Which means every photograph you take with it is a verdict on where you chose to stand.

That sounds like a limitation, and for a week it is. Then it becomes the opposite: it is the only focal length that forces you to solve a picture with your body instead of with your hands. The four photographs below are four walks in Rome, and four things a fifty makes you do.

![A Roman alley before sunrise](/img/foto/7artisans-vicolo-blu.jpg)

## 2. Walk. Then walk a bit more

This is the first rule, and it is most of the job.

With a zoom, when the frame is not working, you change the frame. With a fifty you cannot, so the only thing left is to move — and moving is a far better tool than zooming, because it changes the *relationships* in the picture, not just its size. Step left and the lamp leaves the doorway. Step back and the two walls close around the subject. Step thirty metres down the street and the dome that was hidden behind a cornice now sits exactly at the end of the alley.

That is what happened in the picture above. There is nothing complicated in it: a man with a walking stick, going somewhere, early. What took the time was finding the one position where the two rows of houses funnel towards him, the lamp falls on the stones just ahead of him, and the dome closes the background instead of leaning out of the frame. I did not find that position straight away. I walked past it twice.

**The practical version:** when you lift the camera and the picture is nearly there, do not take it. Take four steps — in any direction — and look again. A fifty punishes the photograph taken from where you happened to be standing, and rewards the one taken from four steps to the left.

![The Tiber towards St Peter's at sunset](/img/foto/7artisans-tevere-san-pietro.jpg)

## 3. When the subject is far away, build a foreground

The second rule solves the problem a fifty creates.

Fifty millimetres cannot reach. Point it at something distant and important — a dome, a mountain, a castle on a hill — and that thing will be small in the frame, because it is small to your eye too. You can either accept a photograph of a small dome in a large nothing, or you can do the one thing that fixes it: **give the picture a strong foreground**.

That is the whole structure of the photograph above. St Peter's is the subject and it is tiny, a silhouette against the light. On its own it would be a postcard taken too far away. What holds the frame up is everything in front of it: the plane leaves hanging into the top of the picture, the bridge across the middle, the cobbles and the two people sitting on the embankment at the bottom. The eye starts near, steps back through the bridge, and arrives at the dome — which now reads as far away *because* the journey to it is visible.

A distant subject alone is small. A distant subject at the end of a foreground is distant, which is a completely different thing.

**The practical version:** when the subject is far, stop looking at it. Turn around, find the branch, the railing, the wall, the stone, the people — and build the picture from your feet outwards. The far thing will take care of itself.

![Tempio di Esculapio, Villa Borghese](/img/foto/7artisans-villa-borghese.jpg)

## 4. Give a big empty surface something to hold on to

The third rule is about the part of the frame you did not choose.

Some surfaces are invasive. Water, sky, snow, sand, an empty square, fog: they take up an enormous share of the picture and give the eye nothing to do with it. They are not neutral — a third of a frame of flat water is a third of a frame the viewer has to cross with nothing to stand on, and the eye crossing it gets bored before it arrives.

The instinct is to crop them out. Usually you can't, and often you shouldn't: in the photograph above the water *is* the reason to be there, because it doubles the temple and the lamps. The answer is not less surface. The answer is to put something in it.

Here that is a rowing boat with two people in it, and the vertical streaks of the lamps breaking the surface into bands. They cost nothing and they change everything:

- they give the eye **reference points** — places to stop and rest while crossing the empty half;
- they give the picture a **present tense**. Something is happening, rather than everything standing still;
- and they give the scale. The boat is what tells you how big the temple is.

**The practical version:** when a flat surface takes over the frame, wait. A boat, a bird, a swimmer, a person walking into the light, a reflection broken by wind — anything alive and moving. The photograph you want is usually the same frame, thirty seconds later.

There is a trap in the opposite direction, too: a long exposure at this hour would have ironed the water flat and smooth. It would have looked clean, and it would have removed the only thing in the lower half worth looking at.

## 5. The aperture is a decision, not a setting

Here is where the lens starts to matter, and where two of the rules above collide.

f/1.8 is why you carry a fast fifty. It buys you the hour when a city is worth photographing — the blue half hour when the lamps are on and the sky is not yet black — without pushing the ISO into the place where a high-resolution file starts to come apart.

But wide open at fifty millimetres, the depth of field is thin. Not artistically thin: *a few centimetres* at close range. And if you have just followed rule two and built a strong foreground, you now have something a metre from the lens and something five hundred metres away, and no single aperture holds both.

So the aperture becomes a decision you make about the picture, not a number you leave where it was:

- **Foreground and background both matter** — stop down to f/5.6 or f/8, raise the ISO, and accept it. Or take two frames, one focused near and one far, and blend them at home.
- **Only the subject matters, and the background is decoration** — open up, and let the lamps behind go soft and round.
- **Low light and nothing in the foreground** — this is the only case where f/1.8 is simply free.

The temple on the lake is the middle case: it is the subject, the water in front of it is a mirror rather than a foreground, and the small lamps at its edge are allowed to melt.

![Steps in Rome at golden hour](/img/foto/7artisans-scalinata.jpg)

## 6. What to ask of the lens itself

Three things decided it for me, and they are the three I would check on any fifty in this class.

**That f/1.8 is usable, not decorative.** Plenty of fast lenses are soft enough wide open that the aperture exists only on the box. This one holds together at f/1.8, which means the hour it buys you is an hour you can actually use.

**That it stays sharp on a demanding sensor.** Sixty-one megapixels resolve past the glass: every softness in the corners is printed at full size with nowhere to hide. A lens that survives that is not being flattered by a forgiving body. This one survived it.

**That the price is in the right place.** What I keep coming back to is the eleven-blade diaphragm — most lenses in this class have seven or nine. You notice the difference the moment a street lamp goes out of focus: a rounder opening keeps points of light round instead of turning them into little cogs. In a city at night, that is not a detail. It is the decision of somebody who thought about what a fifty is actually used for, and spent the money there rather than on a number for the box.

## 7. The discipline

A fifty will not make you a better photographer on its own. What it will do, if you stay with it long enough, is remove the two easiest escapes: you cannot fix a bad position by zooming out, and you cannot rescue a far subject by zooming in.

What is left is walking, and deciding what goes in front.

Those two habits do not stay with the fifty. They follow you back to every other lens you own, which is the real argument for spending a season with one.

---

**The lens in these pictures:** 7Artisans AF 50mm f/1.8, for Sony E, Nikon Z and L mount — [7artisans.store](https://7artisans.store/products/50mm-f1-8-af-lens). Provided for this collaboration; the pictures and the opinions are my own.
